title: The Opium Clerk's Son: Burma, the Aragon Front, and the Farmhouse on Jura
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Motihari, the birth in the opium district
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. City-level coordinate; the birth bungalow survives as a memorial in Motihari but its exact plot is not confirmed by the fetched sources.
stops.campa: In Motihari, in the Champaran district where the Bengal government still grows opium under contract for the China trade, a son is born to Richard Walmesley Blair, sub-deputy agent in the Opium Department, and to Ida Mabel Limouzin, whose family are teak merchants in Burma. They name him Eric Arthur Blair. His father's whole working life is the administration of a drug crop raised by Bihari peasants and sold east at a profit to the Crown. The boy will be taken out of India before he is two and will come back to the empire, in another of its provinces, at nineteen.
suggested_refs: The Blair bungalow at Motihari, restored and opened as a museum in May 2015

stops.name: Henley-on-Thames, the household without a father
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Ida Blair brings Eric and his older sister Marjorie home to England and settles near Henley-on-Thames. Richard stays in Bihar with the opium accounts and does not join them for years. The boy grows up in a household run by women, on the shabby side of the English middle class, in the exact band of income he will later measure to the pound: enough for the forms of gentility, never enough for its substance. At about five he is sent to a small Ursuline convent day school in the town.
suggested_refs: The Thames-side villas of Edwardian Henley, the setting of Coming Up for Air's remembered England

stops.name: Eastbourne, the scholarship boy at St Cyprian's
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (September 1911 to December 1916). Coordinate corrected: one working note carried Eastbourne at negative longitude, which places the school in the Channel; Eastbourne lies east of Greenwich.
stops.campa: At eight he is boarded at St Cyprian's, a preparatory school on Summerdown Road at Eastbourne that takes him at reduced fees because he is clever and can be sold on as a scholarship. He is beaten for wetting the bed, driven hard at Latin and Greek, and taught every day what a boy without money is worth in a house full of boys with it. He wins places at Wellington and at Eton and leaves in December 1916. His own account of the school is written around 1947 and published in 1952, two years after his death.
stops.quote: By the social standards that prevailed about me, I was no good, and could not be any good.
stops.quote_source: George Orwell, 'Such, Such Were the Joys' (written c. 1947, published 1952)
suggested_refs: The site of St Cyprian's, Summerdown Road, Eastbourne, burned down in 1939
sources: orwell.ru library, 'Such, Such Were the Joys'

stops.name: Eton, the King's Scholar who does no work
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (May 1917 to December 1921). One term at Wellington College, January to May 1917, precedes it; a working note gave that stay as a single month and misplaced the college by several kilometres.
stops.campa: He comes up to Eton as a King's Scholar in May 1917, after one term at Wellington College spent waiting for the place to open. Among the seventy Collegers he does the minimum of work and reads enormously, writes for the college papers, and is taught French for a stretch by Aldous Huxley, a temporary master going blind. Cyril Connolly, who was with him at St Cyprian's, is here too. He leaves in December 1921 without sitting for a university scholarship. The family cannot pay for Oxford, and nobody at home suggests that it try.
suggested_refs: College Wall and the scholars' Long Chamber at Eton, where the seventy Collegers lived

stops.name: Southwold, the crammer for the India Office
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month.
stops.campa: His parents have retired to Southwold on the Suffolk coast, and there he is put to a crammer to prepare for the Indian Imperial Police examination. It is his father's road and his mother's family's road; the Limouzins have been in Burma for three generations. He works at riding, at Latin, at the papers, and passes into the service in the summer of 1922. He is posted to Burma, where his grandmother still lives at Moulmein. Whether he wanted any of it, nothing he wrote at the time says.
stops.quote: Failure, failure, failure—failure behind me, failure ahead of me—that was by far the deepest conviction that I carried away.
stops.quote_source: George Orwell, 'Such, Such Were the Joys', on what he took away from St Cyprian's
suggested_refs: The Blair family house on the High Street at Southwold, base for the next decade
sources: orwell.ru library, 'Such, Such Were the Joys'

segments.name: The Indian Imperial Police: Five Years in Burma

stops.name: Rangoon, the landing
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month. Sequence corrected: he sailed on the SS Herefordshire in October 1922 and reached Rangoon in November; the formal appointment follows on 29 November, not before the voyage as one working note had it.
stops.campa: The SS Herefordshire sails in October and lands him at Rangoon in November 1922, nineteen years old, into the service his mother's family has lived beside for three generations. He comes down the gangway into wet heat, pagoda gold over the wharves, and a city where every European he meets outranks every Burmese he meets by arrangement. The Indian Imperial Police is the machinery by which Burma is kept for the Crown, and he has signed five years to work it. He is one of a few hundred European officers in a force holding a province of thirteen million people.
suggested_refs: The Rangoon river wharves and the Strand, first ground of the Burma service

stops.name: Mandalay, the training school and the appointment
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the appointment as Assistant District Superintendent on probation, at 525 rupees a month; training at Mandalay runs through the following months.
stops.campa: At the Police Training School in Mandalay he learns drill, criminal law, Burmese and Hindustani, and comes out fluent enough to take a statement without an interpreter. The town is the old royal capital, taken by the British thirty-seven years earlier and emptied of its king; the palace inside the moat is a barracks and a club. On 29 November 1922 he is gazetted Assistant District Superintendent of Police on probation at five hundred and twenty-five rupees a month, with the power of arrest over a district. He is nineteen.
suggested_refs: Fort Dufferin, the walled Mandalay palace of King Thibaw, in British military use

stops.name: Insein, the prison beside the office
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month. The exact order of the short 1924 postings, Myaungmya, Twante and Syriam, differs between biographies and is not settled here.
stops.campa: By September 1925 he has been through the delta at Myaungmya, held a large subdivision at Twante at twenty-one, and worked at Syriam among the oil refineries. Insein puts him alongside one of the largest prisons in the empire. His duties run to the paperwork of executions and the men waiting on them. 'A Hanging' and 'Shooting an Elephant' come out of these years, written by a man who was wearing the uniform at the time. He stays because an officer who breaks his contract has no money and nothing to go home to.
suggested_refs: Insein Prison, Rangoon district, the colonial gaol he policed toward

stops.name: Moulmein, the family town
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month.
stops.campa: Moulmein on the Salween estuary is a Limouzin town: his maternal grandmother lives here and the family teak business is part of its record. He is twenty-three, in charge of a district, and disliked in the bazaar with a thoroughness he finds petty and completely reasonable. The story he later makes of shooting a working elephant in front of a crowd of thousands, because a white man holding a rifle must not be seen to hesitate, is set in this town. Nine months after arriving he is moved north to Katha.
suggested_refs: The Limouzin family properties at Moulmein and the Kyaikthanlan pagoda above the town

stops.name: Katha, the town that becomes Kyauktada
stops.date_confidence: attested to late 1926, running into 1927; a working note dated this posting 1924, two years early, against the source's own sequence.
stops.campa: Katha stands on the Irrawaddy in Upper Burma: a small station, a European club with a dozen members, a tennis court, a river running brown past the timber yards. It is his last posting and the one he uses whole. Kyauktada, the town of Burmese Days, is Katha with the names changed and the club left standing. He goes down with dengue fever here in 1927. English publishers will refuse the novel for fear that serving officials recognise themselves in it, and Harper will print it first in New York.
suggested_refs: The European club at Katha, model for the club of Burmese Days

stops.name: Southwold, the leave that becomes a resignation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month for the return on medical leave; the resignation is dated 12 March 1928 and is sent from England. One working note reversed the order and had him resign first.
stops.campa: He comes home in July 1927 on medical leave, intending to go back to Burma at the end of it. He does not go back. The resignation goes in and takes effect on 12 March 1928. His father, who gave his own working life to the imperial service and expected his son to keep the family in it, treats the decision as a failure and says so. Eric Blair is twenty-four, with no degree and no profession. He walks the shingle at Southwold out of uniform for the first time in five years.
suggested_refs: The Southwold beach and pier, walked in the summer of the decision

stops.name: Portobello Road, the first expeditions east
stops.date_confidence: attested to the end of 1927; day defaulted to 01. The blue plaque marks the street rather than a confirmed building.
stops.campa: He takes a cheap room off Portobello Road, found for him by the poet Ruth Pitter, and begins going east into the lodging houses and casual wards of the London slums dressed as a tramp, under the name P. S. Burton. He will call it, later, something owed for Burma. He sleeps in spikes, eats in the cheap kitchens, and learns the vocabulary and the etiquette of destitution, neither of which a change of clothes supplies. Then he comes back west to the room, washes, and writes it up.
suggested_refs: The casual wards of the London workhouses, entered under the name P. S. Burton

stops.name: Rue du Pot-de-Fer, the room in the fifth arrondissement
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, with the move placed in early 1928; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: In early 1928 he moves to Paris, to a working-class street in the fifth arrondissement a few doors from his aunt Nellie Limouzin and her Esperantist partner Eugene Lanti. He writes novels nobody buys and stories nobody prints. When the money goes he takes work as a plongeur, seventeen hours a day in the heat under a hotel dining room, scraping plates in a cellar. The novels come to nothing. The cellar becomes Down and Out in Paris and London, published five years later.
stops.quote: THE rue du Coq d'Or, Paris, seven in the morning. A succession of furious, choking yells from the street.
stops.quote_source: George Orwell, Down and Out in Paris and London (1933), opening line
suggested_refs: 6 rue du Pot-de-Fer, Paris 5e, the lodging behind the rue Mouffetard market
sources: gutenberg.net.au, Down and Out in Paris and London

stops.name: Paris, the first article anybody pays for
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Pinned to the canonical Paris coordinate; the paper's own office address is not established here.
stops.campa: On 6 October 1928 the Paris paper Monde prints an article on censorship in England by an unknown Englishman signing himself E. A. Blair. It is the first piece of writing he is paid for. His argument is that English writers are governed less by law than by an unwritten agreement among publishers and public about what may be said, a mechanism harder to point at than a censor and better at the work. He is twenty-five and living on a few francs a day.
suggested_refs: Monde, the Paris weekly founded by Henri Barbusse, issue of 6 October 1928

stops.name: Hopital Cochin, the free ward
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month. Coordinate corrected to the hospital on the boulevard de Port-Royal; a working note placed it some three hundred metres east on the Val-de-Grace block.
stops.campa: In February he goes down with pneumonia and is taken to the Hopital Cochin on the boulevard de Port-Royal, a free public hospital where the poor of Paris are treated in long open wards and used for teaching. Students come round the beds in files and examine him in front of one another. He watches a man die in the next bed and nobody notice for some time. Seventeen years later he sets it down as 'How the Poor Die', and does not soften what a charity ward was in 1929.
suggested_refs: The nineteenth-century open wards of the Hopital Cochin, 47 boulevard de Port-Royal

stops.name: Southwold, two lives at once
stops.date_confidence: attested to the end of 1929; the tramping and hop-picking run through 1930 and 1931.
stops.campa: Broke, he comes back to his parents' house at Southwold at the end of 1929 and spends two years living in two countries at once. He tutors backward boys and takes tea with the town; then he walks out with a bundle to sleep in casual wards and pick hops in Kent for a few shillings a week, coming back with his hands stained black from the bines. The Adelphi begins printing him. 'The Spike', a night in a workhouse ward set down flat, appears in April 1931, over the name Eric Blair.
suggested_refs: The Kent hop gardens worked in the picking seasons of 1930 and 1931

stops.name: Hayes, the schoolmaster and the pen name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month for The Hawthorns. The move to the larger Frays College at Uxbridge belongs to 1933, not 1932 as one working note had it, and pneumonia ends the teaching by January 1934.
stops.campa: He takes a post at The Hawthorns, a private school for twenty boys in Hayes, and teaches in a Middlesex suburb of new brick and arterial road. On 9 January 1933 Victor Gollancz publishes Down and Out in Paris and London. Eric Blair does not want his parents to find their name on a book about washing dishes and sleeping in spikes, and takes a pseudonym out of a Suffolk river and the patron saint of England. He moves to Frays College at Uxbridge later that year, and pneumonia puts him in hospital and ends the schoolmastering in January 1934.
suggested_refs: The River Orwell in Suffolk, one half of the chosen name

stops.name: Hampstead, the bookshop counter
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (October 1934 to January 1936). The party at which he met Eileen O'Shaughnessy is placed in London in 1935 without an address; it is pinned here, near his Hampstead lodgings, for want of a better location.
stops.campa: From October 1934 he works part-time at Booklovers' Corner on South End Road in Hampstead, mornings for writing and afternoons behind the counter among the stamp collectors and the customers who order books and never come back for them. Harper brings out Burmese Days in New York on 25 October; Gollancz, who feared a libel action, follows in England the next June. At a party given by Rosalind Obermeyer in 1935 he meets Eileen O'Shaughnessy, who read English at St Hugh's College, Oxford, and is now a graduate student in psychology. They marry the following June.
suggested_refs: Booklovers' Corner, South End Road, Hampstead, and the essay 'Bookshop Memories'

stops.name: Wigan, the room over the tripe shop
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; he leaves London on 31 January 1936. Correction: the trip was not commissioned for the Left Book Club, which was not founded until May 1936; Gollancz suggested the journey and the Club published the result in 1937.
stops.campa: Gollancz has suggested he go north and look at what unemployment does. He leaves London on 31 January 1936 and works through Coventry, Manchester, Wigan, Barnsley and Sheffield with a notebook, counting rents, measuring rooms, writing down what a miner eats in a week. The Special Branch opens a file on him during this journey and keeps it open for the rest of his life. In Wigan he lodges over a tripe shop, in a bed in a shared room, above a cellar where uncut tripe lies under the dust.
suggested_refs: The Wigan lodging house over the tripe shop, opening scene of The Road to Wigan Pier

stops.name: Bryn Hall, the crawl to the coal face
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the exact day of the descent is not fixed here.
stops.campa: He goes down Bryn Hall pit and then travels the underground road to the working face on his hands and knees, along a passage too low to stand in, for the better part of a mile. At the face men strip to the waist and hew in dust with the roof a foot above their backs. He is six foot three. Nothing in his life so far has been physical work of that order, and he says so in the book without pretending otherwise. He comes up unable to walk properly for a day afterwards.
suggested_refs: Bryn Hall colliery near Wigan, descended in February 1936

stops.name: Wallington, the marriage and the village shop
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinate corrected: a working note put Wallington some eight kilometres east of the village, in open farmland.
stops.campa: On 9 June 1936 Eric Blair marries Eileen O'Shaughnessy in the parish church of St Mary at Wallington, a Hertfordshire village of a few hundred people. They live at The Stores, a cottage with a shop counter at the front from which Eileen sells groceries and sweets to the village while he writes at the back. They keep goats and hens. The Road to Wigan Pier is finished in this cottage in December, and within a few weeks of finishing it he leaves for Spain.
suggested_refs: The Stores at Wallington, cottage and village shop, rented from 1936

segments.name: Spain: The Militia, the May Days, the Bullet

stops.name: Barcelona, the Lenin Barracks
stops.date_confidence: attested for the departure from England on 23 December 1936; the Barcelona arrival is placed at the end of December. Barracks coordinate approximate to the central city; no street address is established here.
stops.campa: He crosses into Spain at the end of December meaning to write newspaper articles, and enlists in a militia within days instead. Barcelona is under workers' control: shops collectivised, churches gutted, tipping abolished, waiters looking customers in the face, everybody addressing everybody as comrade. At the Lenin Barracks he is drilled with recruits who have no rifles to drill with. In the guardroom an Italian militiaman, a stranger who will be dead within the year for all he knows, looks at him and puts out a hand.
stops.quote: As we went out he stepped across the room and gripped my hand very hard.
stops.quote_source: George Orwell, Homage to Catalonia (1938), ch. 1, on the Italian militiaman in the Lenin Barracks guardroom
suggested_refs: The Lenin Barracks, Barcelona, POUM depot and drill ground in the winter of 1936

stops.name: Alcubierre, the winter trenches
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The ILP contingent goes up to the Aragon front near Alcubierre in January, into trenches at fifteen hundred feet in the worst of the winter. The fascist line is a valley's width away, close enough to shout across and too far to hit with what they have. There are almost no rifles worth firing and no shells to fire, and five hours go to gathering firewood for every hour of soldiering. Lice live in every seam of every man. He is colder here than he has ever been anywhere in his life.
stops.quote: the characteristic smell of war — in my experience a smell of excrement and decaying food
suggested_refs: The parapet positions above Alcubierre, Aragon front, winter of 1937

stops.name: Barcelona, the rooftop in the May Days
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the outbreak of the fighting, 3 to 7 May 1937. The specific hotel, the Continental, comes from the dossier and is tagged [R]; the fetched biography confirms the episode but not the address, which supplies this pin.
stops.campa: On leave in Barcelona in May he finds the city turned around: the revolutionary posters still up and the revolution itself being taken apart by the Communist-aligned government he is nominally fighting for. On 3 May assault guards move on the anarchist-held telephone exchange and the city goes to the barricades. For four days he keeps watch with a rifle on a roof above the Ramblas, guarding a POUM building against men on his own side, while Eileen works on at the ILP office. The English press reports the week as a fascist rising.
stops.quote: atrocities are believed in or disbelieved in solely on grounds of political predilection
stops.quote_source: George Orwell, 'Looking Back on the Spanish War' (1943)
suggested_refs: The Telefonica building on the Placa de Catalunya, seized 3 May 1937
sources: orwell.ru library, 'Looking Back on the Spanish War'

stops.name: The Huesca front, shot through the throat
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Spanish-language biography, at about five in the morning on 20 May 1937. Contradiction flagged: one working note dated the wounding 27 May, which is in fact the date of the onward transfer from Lleida to Tarragona.
stops.campa: Back at the front outside Huesca, at about five in the morning on 20 May, standing at his full height in the trench at the changing of the guard, he is shot through the throat by a sniper. The bullet passes between the carotid artery and the windpipe and misses the spine. He is carried down to the field hospital at Sietamo on a stretcher, unable to make a sound above a whisper. The doctors tell him he will not speak again. A vocal cord is destroyed and the voice never comes back to full strength. He is finished as a soldier.
stops.quote_source: George Orwell, Homage to Catalonia (1938), ch. 5: what he would have answered if asked what he was fighting for
suggested_refs: The forward positions at Monte Oscuro and before Huesca, held by the ILP contingent in May 1937

stops.name: Lleida, the hospital and the road back
stops.date_confidence: attested to about 22 May for the Lleida admission, with the onward move to Tarragona dated 27 May 1937. A working note dated the Lleida stop itself to the 27th, conflating admission and transfer.
stops.campa: From Sietamo he goes back through Barbastro to the hospital at Lleida, then on 27 May to Tarragona, and two days after that to a sanatorium outside Barcelona. Every move takes him further from the line and nearer to the political trap closing behind him. The doctors at Lleida have seen many throats like his and tell him nothing can be done about the paralysed cord. He writes letters instead of talking. He has been in Spain five months and at the front for four of them.
suggested_refs: The wartime hospital at Lleida, stage on the evacuation from the Aragon front

stops.name: Barcelona, the sanatorium and the flight
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the admission to the POUM sanatorium; the discharge as medically unfit and the crossing into France follow in June 1937.
stops.campa: He convalesces at a POUM sanatorium outside Barcelona and is discharged as unfit for further service. In June the POUM is outlawed and its members arrested wherever they are found, and the militia he served in is reclassified overnight as a fascist fifth column. The government he was holding a trench for is now the one looking for him. He and Eileen sleep out of their hotel, move separately, and get over the French border with their passports and nothing else.
stops.quote: I remember saying once to Arthur Koestler, 'History stopped in 1936'
stops.quote_source: George Orwell, 'Looking Back on the Spanish War' (1943)
suggested_refs: The Maurin Sanatorium, the POUM convalescent house outside Barcelona
sources: orwell.ru library, 'Looking Back on the Spanish War'

stops.name: Valencia, the deposition against the Blairs
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Orwell was not present: he and Eileen had been out of Spain for some weeks. The pin marks where the document was filed, not where he stood. Place corrected: a working note gave Barcelona; the Tribunal for Espionage and High Treason sat at Valencia, and the trial in absentia followed at Barcelona in late 1938.
stops.campa: On 13 July 1937 a deposition is laid before the Tribunal for Espionage and High Treason at Valencia naming Eric Blair and Eileen Blair as rabid Trotskyists and agents of the POUM. By the date on the paper they have been out of the country for weeks. The charge rests on no act, no meeting and no evidence beyond the militia they served in, and it is filed by the government whose front line he was holding when the sniper found him. A trial follows at Barcelona in October and November 1938, in their absence.
stops.quote: I saw newspaper reports which did not bear any relation to the facts, not even the relationship which is implied in an ordinary lie.
stops.quote_source: George Orwell, 'Looking Back on the Spanish War' (1943), section IV, on press coverage of the Spanish war generally
suggested_refs: The 13 July 1937 deposition to the Tribunal for Espionage and High Treason, Valencia
sources: orwell.ru library, 'Looking Back on the Spanish War'

segments.name: The Stores, the Sanatorium, and Marrakesh

stops.name: Wallington, writing Homage to Catalonia
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1937 for the return and the writing; publication by Secker and Warburg is dated April 1938.
stops.campa: He is back at the cottage in July and starts Homage to Catalonia at once, writing fast, arguing about troop dispositions and newspaper lies while both are still hot. The Road to Wigan Pier had come out from the Left Book Club earlier that year, while he was in Spain. Gollancz refuses the new book unread, on the ground of what it says about the Communists, and so ends the arrangement that has published everything of his since 1933. Secker and Warburg bring it out in April 1938. It sells poorly.
stops.quote: Every line of serious work that I have written since 1936 has been written, directly or indirectly, against totalitarianism and for democratic socialism.
suggested_refs: Homage to Catalonia, Secker and Warburg, April 1938, first edition

stops.name: Aylesford, Preston Hall sanatorium
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month, with the stay running March to September 1938. The essay written on joining the Independent Labour Party is 'Why I Join the I.L.P.', New Leader, 24 June 1938; one working note gave a past-tense title that does not exist.
stops.campa: In March a lung haemorrhage puts him in Preston Hall, a Royal British Legion sanatorium at Aylesford in Kent. He is there six months, forbidden to work for much of it. The doctors record bronchiectasis; he has had a bad chest since infancy and no one can fix the date the tuberculosis took hold. From the sanatorium in June he joins the Independent Labour Party and gives his reasons in the New Leader, which are that the choice is narrowing to fascism or a socialism worth the name, and that the time for standing outside parties is running out.
suggested_refs: 'Why I Join the I.L.P.', New Leader, 24 June 1938

stops.name: Marrakesh, the winter on the Casablanca road
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of departure, with the Moroccan stay running to March 1939. A lease from 15 October 1938 at 550 francs a month is reported in the dossier and is not independently verified here.
stops.campa: The Blairs leave England in September for the sake of his lungs and rent a villa outside Marrakesh on the Casablanca road. They stay a little over six months. He writes Coming Up for Air here, a novel about an insurance salesman who drives back to look for the England of his childhood and finds it built over. He also writes 'Marrakech', in which he watches an old woman going by under a load of firewood and records exactly how long it took him to notice that she was there.
suggested_refs: The rented villa on the Casablanca road outside Marrakesh, October 1938 to March 1939

stops.name: Casablanca, the passage home
stops.date_confidence: attested only as far as the return to England on 30 March 1939; a departure date of 26 March circulates but is not carried by the fetched source. Month kept, day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: They sail from Casablanca at the end of March and are back in England on the thirtieth. The crossing takes the last of the money. He has a finished novel in his luggage and half a year of Moroccan sun in him, and he comes home to a country being fitted for gas masks and digging shelters in its gardens. Coming Up for Air is published in June. In September the war he has been arguing about in print for three years begins, and he offers himself for military service and is refused on medical grounds.
suggested_refs: The port of Casablanca, embarkation for Europe in March 1939

stops.name: Broadcasting House, the Eastern Service
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month. End date corrected: he resigned from the BBC in September 1943, not November as one working note had it; Tribune follows in November 1943.
stops.campa: In August 1941 he joins the BBC Eastern Service as a Talks Producer, making programmes in English for India while the Japanese come up through Burma and the Quit India movement gathers. He commissions T. S. Eliot, E. M. Forster and Mulk Raj Anand, writes news commentary to a censor's guidance, and knows the audience is small to the point of invisibility. He calls the two years wasted. In Horizon that same month he prints 'Wells, Hitler and the World State', taking apart the rationalist optimism of H. G. Wells, who spent forty years promising a scientific world order and lived to watch the aeroplane and the radio go to work for Hitler.
stops.quote: Political language — and with variations this is true of all political parties, from Conservatives to Anarchists — is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable
stops.quote_source: George Orwell, 'Politics and the English Language' (1946)
suggested_refs: 'Wells, Hitler and the World State', Horizon, August 1941
sources: orwell.ru library, 'Politics and the English Language'

stops.name: Kilburn, the flying bomb on Mortimer Crescent
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month for the V-1 strike; the adoption of Richard Horatio Blair is dated 14 May 1944. The detail of the crumpled Animal Farm typescript recovered from the rubble is widely repeated and is tagged [R].
stops.campa: In May the Blairs adopt a boy of three weeks and name him Richard Horatio Blair. A month later a V-1 comes down on Mortimer Crescent in Kilburn and takes the front off the flat. Nobody is hurt. Orwell goes back into the wreckage again and again with a wheelbarrow and brings his books out through the plaster dust a barrow-load at a time, along the Kilburn High Road. The typescript of Animal Farm, finished in February and by then refused by four publishers, comes out of the rubble creased and still legible.
suggested_refs: 10a Mortimer Crescent, Kilburn, struck by a V-1 in June 1944

stops.name: Canonbury Square, Tribune and the weekly column
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1944 for the move to 27b Canonbury Square; month and day set to order the segment. He becomes literary editor of Tribune in November 1943 and leaves the staff post in early 1945.
stops.campa: The family moves into a top-floor flat at 27b Canonbury Square in Islington. He is literary editor of Tribune, the weekly of the Labour left, and writes 'As I Please', a column about whatever he likes. He turns it out every week while running a books page and reviewing on top of that, and nobody at the paper tells him what to put in it. The subjects run to the price of a wedding ring, the behaviour of book reviewers, English cooking, nationalism, sixpenny paperbacks, and the toads that come up out of the ground in spring.
stops.quote: Good prose is like a windowpane.
suggested_refs: The 'As I Please' columns, Tribune, 1943 to 1947

stops.name: Newcastle upon Tyne, the death of Eileen Blair
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, at Fernwood House nursing home; the inquest returned death from cardiac failure under ether and chloroform properly administered.
stops.campa: Eileen Blair goes into a nursing home at Newcastle upon Tyne for a hysterectomy. She dies under the anaesthetic. The inquest finds cardiac failure under ether and chloroform properly administered, and returns no fault. She is thirty-nine. Orwell is in Europe reporting for the Observer and cannot be reached quickly. Their adopted son is not yet a year old. They had been married eight years and nine months, and he had spent most of the last of them abroad.
suggested_refs: Fernwood House nursing home, Newcastle upon Tyne, 29 March 1945

stops.name: Canonbury Square, Animal Farm published
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. T. S. Eliot's rejection letter for Faber is widely quoted and is tagged [R] here, having not been re-verified in this pass.
stops.campa: Secker and Warburg publish Animal Farm on 17 August 1945, four publishers having turned it down while the Soviet Union was an ally and a reader at the Ministry of Information having advised against it. T. S. Eliot, refusing it for Faber, had observed that the pigs were the cleverest animals and therefore the best qualified to run the farm. The first printing sells out at once and the book goes on selling. He is forty-two, a widower with an infant son. For the first time in his life he has money.
suggested_refs: Animal Farm: A Fairy Story, Secker and Warburg, 17 August 1945

segments.name: Barnhill: The Island and the Book

stops.name: Barnhill, the farmhouse at the north end of Jura
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; he first visited Jura in September 1945 and the residence runs to January 1949. Coordinate corrected: a working note placed Barnhill some sixteen kilometres out in the Sound of Jura.
stops.campa: In May 1946 he takes Barnhill, a farmhouse at the north end of the Isle of Jura, twenty-five miles from the ferry with the last seven of them on a track. There is no electricity and no telephone. He brings his sister Avril and his son, grows vegetables, fishes, shoots rabbits, cuts peat, and writes upstairs beside a paraffin stove. Visitors remark on the cold and on how well he looks. He has a diseased lung and he has chosen an island in the Hebrides to keep it in.
stops.quote: But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.
stops.quote_source: George Orwell, 'Politics and the English Language' (1946)
suggested_refs: Barnhill, Ardlussa parish, Isle of Jura, and the track from Ardlussa

stops.name: The Gulf of Corryvreckan, the boat in the whirlpool
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the episode is carried in the fetched biography and is promoted here from the dossier's [R] tagging. The detail of the islet and the passing lobster boat is standard in the biographies and not separately re-verified.
stops.campa: On 19 August he takes a small boat out through the Gulf of Corryvreckan with his son and his sister's family, misreads the tide table by an hour, and puts the party into the race at the wrong state of the water. The outboard motor is torn off the transom. They row for an islet, the boat goes over as they reach it, and three-year-old Richard is pulled out from under the hull. They are marooned until a passing lobster boat takes them off. He goes back to Barnhill and gets on with the novel.
suggested_refs: The Corryvreckan whirlpool between Jura and Scarba, and the islet of Eilean Mor

stops.name: Barnhill, the first draft finished in bed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the completion of the first draft of the novel then called The Last Man in Europe.
stops.campa: On 7 November 1947 he finishes the first draft of the book he has been calling The Last Man in Europe, in bed at Barnhill, coughing blood. It has taken him a year and a half between illnesses. The typescript is filthy with correction and no typist within a hundred miles will come out to the house to take it. He will retype the whole of it himself, propped on pillows, in the last months before it goes to London. Six weeks after finishing the draft he is admitted to hospital.
stops.quote: All writers are vain, selfish, and lazy, and at the very bottom of their motives there lies a mystery.
suggested_refs: The upstairs bedroom at Barnhill, where both drafts of Nineteen Eighty-Four were typed

stops.name: East Kilbride, streptomycin at Hairmyres
stops.date_confidence: attested to the week before Christmas 1947, with the stay running to July 1948; the streptomycin course begins 19 or 20 February 1948 and is stopped after fifty days. Coordinate corrected to the hospital; a working note gave the East Kilbride town centre.
stops.campa: A week before Christmas 1947 he is admitted to Hairmyres Hospital at East Kilbride with tuberculosis in the left lung. David Astor arranges an import licence and pays for streptomycin out of the United States, at that date almost unobtainable in Britain. The course begins on 19 or 20 February 1948, the first given to any patient in Scotland. His hair falls out, his nails lift, his mouth ulcerates and his throat blisters until he cannot swallow. After fifty days the drug is stopped. The unused remainder is given to two other patients on the ward, and cures them.
suggested_refs: Hairmyres Hospital, East Kilbride, and the first Scottish course of streptomycin

stops.name: Cranham, the chalet, the list, and publication day
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1949 for the admission, with the stay running to September; Celia Kirwan's visit for the Information Research Department is dated 29 March 1949 and publication 8 June 1949. The Gandhi essay in Partisan Review, January 1949, is a standard bibliographic fact carried here as [R], not re-verified in this pass.
stops.campa: In January 1949 he leaves Jura for the last time and enters the Cotswold Sanatorium at Cranham, a row of wooden chalets on a Gloucestershire hillside, and never sees Barnhill again. Partisan Review prints his essay on Gandhi that month, which begins by refusing saints the benefit of the doubt and ends by granting him almost everything else. On 29 March Celia Kirwan comes from the Foreign Office's Information Research Department, and he gives her a list of writers he thinks unreliable. Nineteen Eighty-Four is published on 8 June while he lies there.
suggested_refs: The Cotswold Sanatorium chalets at Cranham, Gloucestershire

segments.name: University College Hospital and the Grave

stops.name: University College Hospital, the bedside marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; he was transferred to the hospital in September 1949. The crimson smoking jacket and David Astor as best man are standard in the biographies and tagged [R].
stops.campa: He is moved to University College Hospital in September and married there on 13 October to Sonia Brownell, editorial assistant at Horizon, in a ceremony at the bedside. He wears a crimson corduroy smoking jacket over pyjamas. David Astor stands as best man. She is thirty-one and he is forty-six, and he is making arrangements to be flown to a sanatorium in the Swiss Alps in January. The wedding party goes on to lunch at the Ritz without the groom, who cannot leave the bed.
suggested_refs: University College Hospital, Gower Street, room 65

stops.name: University College Hospital, the artery in the lung
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; death from a massive pulmonary haemorrhage in the early hours of 21 January 1950.
stops.campa: In the early hours of 21 January 1950 an artery bursts in his lung and he dies in his room at University College Hospital. He is forty-six. The charter flight to Switzerland was booked for the following week and a new fishing rod stood in the corner, bought for the convalescence he expected to have. His will asks that no biography of him be written. Sonia Orwell, his wife of three months, becomes his literary executor and spends the next thirty years administering the refusal.
suggested_refs: The fishing rod ordered for the Swiss convalescence, and the will of 18 January 1950

stops.name: Sutton Courtenay, the stone that says Eric Arthur Blair
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinate corrected to the church itself; two working notes placed the grave several hundred metres outside the churchyard.
stops.campa: He asked to be buried according to the rites of the Church of England in the nearest convenient cemetery, and he had no church and no village of his own. David Astor, who lived nearby, found the plot. On 26 January he is buried in the churchyard of All Saints at Sutton Courtenay in Oxfordshire, in ground he never walked in life. The headstone gives his legal name and his dates and nothing else: it does not say George Orwell and it does not say that he wrote anything. A few yards off lies H. H. Asquith.
suggested_refs: The grave of Eric Arthur Blair, All Saints' churchyard, Sutton Courtenay, marked by a rose bush
